title: SpectraLLM: Uncovering the Ability of LLMs for Molecule Structure Elucidation from Multi-Spectra
claim: Heterogeneous inputs are converted into text prompts and fed to a frozen LLM with LoRA adapters to generate structured outputs.
layout: Bottom-to-top flow: inputs, prompt tokens, backbone plus LoRA, output panel; decoder-stack inset left
description: The figure shows a bottom-to-top training pipeline. A purple dashed box at the bottom holds six small spectrum plots (IR, Raman, UV-Vis, C/H NMR, HSQC NMR, Mass), each with extracted peak values as text beneath it. Above them is a row of purple token squares and a chat-template prompt string, with green system-prompt and blue human-prompt text. Large arrows lead up to an orange 'Backbone: Pretrained Weights W' block, marked with a snowflake to show it is frozen. It is paired with yellow trapezoids for the LoRA matrices A and B, marked with flames to show they are trained. A gradient 'LoRA Combination' bar sits across the top. An arrow leads to a blue dashed 'Predicted Molecule' box containing a SMILES string and a skeletal structure. A zoomed inset on the left shows the stacked decoder layers. The eye goes first to the large orange backbone block.
caption: Overview of the training pipeline for structure elucidation. Characteristic spectral peaks are extracted from raw IR, Raman, UV, NMR, or MS data and used to construct natural language prompts. These are input to a frozen large language model fine-tuned via LoRA. The model is trained to autoregressively generate molecular structures in SMILES format, supervised by the ground-truth sequence.
abstract: Automated molecular structure elucidation remains challenging, as existing approaches often depend on pre-compiled databases or restrict themselves to single spectroscopic modalities. Here we introduce SpectraLLM, a large language model that performs end-to-end structure prediction by reasoning over one or multiple spectra. Unlike conventional spectrum-to-structure pipelines, SpectraLLM represents both continuous (IR, Raman, UV-Vis, NMR) and discrete (MS) modalities in a shared language space, enabling it to capture substructural patterns that are complementary across different spectral types. We pretrain and fine-tune the model on small-molecule domains and evaluate it on four public benchmark datasets. SpectraLLM achieves state-of-the-art performance, substantially surpassing single-modality baselines. Moreover, it demonstrates strong robustness in unimodal settings and further improves prediction accuracy when jointly reasoning over diverse spectra, establishing a scalable paradigm for language-based spectroscopic analysis. Code is available at https://github.com/OPilgrim/SpectraLLM.
